title: Andes Virus Exposure and Nosocomial Transmission Events to Healthcare Personnel: A Systematic Review.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) is a high-consequence infectious disease with substantial mortality. On 2 May 2026, the World Health Organization reported a multinational ANDV outbreak, raising questions regarding the risk of transmission to healthcare personnel (HCP). METHODS: We performed a systematic review per PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO:CRD420261283806) for studies describing healthcare-associated ANDV exposure or transmission events to HCP. RESULTS: Eight studies reporting on 7 events were included, describing a total of 17 healthcare-associated cases. Overall, 207 individuals were exposed, including 118 HCP, resulting in 8 infections and 4 deaths among HCP. Studies describing HCP infections reported none or inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. CONCLUSIONS: Transmission of ANDV to HCP has been reported in the setting of delayed implementation of transmission-based precautions or breaches in infection control practice. Limitations in published exposure events highlight the need for standardized reporting of exposure events and outcomes as well as infection prevention measures implemented.

title: Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany.
abstract: A critical, annotated version of Narlikar’s iconic novel about a cybervirus attack by an advanced alien species—with updated text and added material. A year before Robin Cook’s Invasion (1997)—in which an alien force activates a latent biological virus in humans—and almost a decade before Liu Cixin’s The Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy (2008–2010)—in which humanity’s scientific progress is curtailed by an alien supercomputer’s “sophon-lock”—Jayant Vishnu Narlikar’s Virus (1996) painted a similar scenario. In his novel, a cybervirus broadcast by an advanced, extraterrestrial species invades Earth and freezes its digital infrastructure: a prelude to an alien invasion. The novel, first published in Marathi, recounts how vast radio arrays on Earth intercept a seemingly innocuous message from an unknown planet orbiting Barnard’s Star. The radio signal, sent six years prior, coalesces into a cybervirus that has the potential to cause a complete digital meltdown and lead humanity into an age of chaos—an alien first strike to prevent humanity from evolving further. This book—a critical, annotated version of Virus, edited and revised by Sami Ahmad Khan—reissues Narlikar’s iconic novel with updated text and added dimensions. It includes detailed annotations that locate the technology of the text along the axis of contemporary scientific thought, as well as critical essays that focus on the literary, political, and sociocultural dimensions of the novel; essays on Narlikar’s role in India’s science and science fiction; an exclusive conversation with the author; bibliographical information on his works; and a bonus short story. Contributions by Sami Ahmad Khan, Nilam Ingole, Priteegandha Naik, Jayant V. Narlikar, and Dibyadyuti Roy.

source_records.abstract: Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus-infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the presence and characteristics of Hantaviruses in pet rats in Germany, addressing the need to understand zoonotic transmission risks and the epidemiology of these viruses in domesticated animals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in Germany between 2022 and 2024, focusing on pet rats from various regions. A total of 1,200 pet rats were sampled, and their presence of Hantaviruses was analyzed.

source_body_en: A critical, annotated version of Narlikar’s iconic novel about a cybervirus attack by an advanced alien species—with updated text and added material. A year before Robin Cook’s Invasion (1997)—in which an alien force activates a latent biological virus in humans—and almost a decade before Liu Cixin’s The Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy (2008–2010)—in which humanity’s scientific progress is curtailed by an alien supercomputer’s “sophon-lock”—Jayant Vishnu Narlikar’s Virus (1996) painted a similar scenario. In his novel, a cybervirus broadcast by an advanced, extraterrestrial species invades Earth and freezes its digital infrastructure: a prelude to an alien invasion. The novel, first published in Marathi, recounts how vast radio arrays on Earth intercept a seemingly innocuous message from an unknown planet orbiting Barnard’s Star. The radio signal, sent six years prior, coalesces into a cybervirus that has the potential to cause a complete digital meltdown and lead humanity into an age of chaos—an alien first strike to prevent humanity from evolving further. This book—a critical, annotated version of Virus, edited and revised by Sami Ahmad Khan—reissues Narlikar’s iconic novel with updated text and added dimensions. It includes detailed annotations that locate the technology of the text along the axis of contemporary scientific thought, as well as critical essays that focus on the literary, political, and sociocultural dimensions of the novel; essays on Narlikar’s role in India’s science and science fiction; an exclusive conversation with the author; bibliographical information on his works; and a bonus short story. Contributions by Sami Ahmad Khan, Nilam Ingole, Priteegandha Naik, Jayant V. Narlikar, and Dibyadyuti Roy.

title: Learning from COVID-19 to strengthen hantavirus preparedness and public health response
abstract: Years after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the world continues to face significant health, social, and economic challenges, while emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases remain a growing global public health concern. This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. COVID-19 spreads efficiently between humans and caused a global pandemic, whereas Hantavirus infections are mainly transmitted from rodents to humans and remain geographically localized despite a higher case fatality rate. While vaccines are available for COVID-19, none exist for Hantavirus disease. The study also highlights the value of artificial intelligence, epidemic intelligence, and the One Health approach for improving outbreak prediction, detection, and surveillance.

title: Framing Krisis Hantavirus dalam Komunikasi Pemasaran Pariwisata
abstract: This study examines how English-language online media in Indonesia frame the hantavirus crisis involving MV Hondius and how such framing is relevant to tourism marketing communication during a transnational health crisis. Using qualitative content analysis and framing analysis, the study analyzes 16 unique and relevant news articles archived from Jakarta Globe and The Jakarta Post between 4 and 31 May 2026 with the keywords “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, and “Andes virus”. The corpus was selected from 27 initial publications through purposive sampling, relevance screening, and deduplication. The articles were coded according to publication phase, dominant frame, actor visibility, risk emphasis, and marketing communication implications. The findings show that the news did not merely report a medical event but constructed a crisis narrative that moved from outbreak escalation to cross-border control and reputational normalization. The dominant frame was cross-national governance, followed by reputational recovery, tourism mobility, and health threat. The study argues that tourism crisis messages should combine health accuracy, mobility transparency, destination reassurance, and evidence-based reputation recovery within an eco-systemic crisis communication perspective.

elements_en.study_design_and_population: Using qualitative content analysis and framing analysis, the study analyzes 16 unique and relevant news articles archived from Jakarta Globe and The Jakarta Post between 4 and 31 May 2026 with the keywords “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, and “Andes virus”.
elements_en.methods: The corpus was selected from 27 initial publications through purposive sampling, relevance screening, and deduplication. The articles were coded according to publication phase, dominant frame, actor visibility, risk emphasis, and marketing communication implications.
elements_en.main_results: The findings show that the news did not merely report a medical event but constructed a crisis narrative that moved from outbreak escalation to cross-border control and reputational normalization.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The dominant frame was cross-national governance, followed by reputational recovery, tourism mobility, and health threat. title: Long-term epidemiology of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across three endemic clusters in Jiangxi Province, China’s middle Yangtze River region, 2005–2024
abstract: Abstract Background Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) burden and epidemiological patterns vary across endemic areas of Jiangxi Province. We compared long-term epidemiological patterns in three predefined clusters and explored county-level incidence changes following vaccination-programme initiation. Methods This retrospective ecological study analysed surveillance and population data for 27 counties during 2005–2024. We described burden and seasonality, assessed annual trends with Joinpoint regression, and examined observed age-specific rates alongside complementary age–period–cohort (APC) summaries. In an exploratory analysis of adults aged 15–59 years across all 27 counties, we estimated the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) over a balanced event-year 0–4 window using the Callaway–Sant’Anna group-time estimator. Counties received equal observation weights; not-yet-initiating and non-initiating counties served as comparisons. Results Across the clusters, 7,570 HFRS cases were reported. Mean annual crude incidence was 7.00, 2.43, and 1.25 per 100,000 person-years in Clusters I–III, respectively; corresponding Segi-standardised rates were 6.29, 2.03, and 1.09. All three clusters had winter peaks, with additional May–June elevations in Clusters I and II. Only Cluster I showed a statistically significant decline in age-standardised incidence over 2005–2024 (average annual percentage change − 4.28%; 95% confidence interval [CI] − 7.27 to − 2.18). Adults aged ≥ 60 years had the highest incidence among the three broad age groups in each cluster, and incidence in this group increased on average in Cluster III. APC period rate ratios were lower in 2020–2024 than in 2010–2014 across all three clusters, with non-linear cohort variation identified in Cluster I. The vaccination-programme initiation ATT among adults aged 15–59 years was − 1.208 cases per 100,000 (95% CI − 1.994 to − 0.421). Conclusions HFRS burden, seasonality, and age-specific incidence differed across the three clusters. Vaccination-programme initiation was associated with lower county-level incidence in the exploratory analysis. These findings support surveillance and prevention tailored to local burden and seasonal patterns, with continued attention to adults aged ≥ 60 years.

source_body_en: Abstract Background Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) burden and epidemiological patterns vary across endemic areas of Jiangxi Province. We compared long-term epidemiological patterns in three predefined clusters and explored county-level incidence changes following vaccination-programme initiation. Methods This retrospective ecological study analysed surveillance and population data for 27 counties during 2005–2024. We described burden and seasonality, assessed annual trends with Joinpoint regression, and examined observed age-specific rates alongside complementary age–period–cohort (APC) summaries. In an exploratory analysis of adults aged 15–59 years across all 27 counties, we estimated the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) over a balanced event-year 0–4 window using the Callaway–Sant’Anna group-time estimator. Counties received equal observation weights; not-yet-initiating and non-initiating counties served as comparisons. Results Across the clusters, 7,570 HFRS cases were reported. Mean annual crude incidence was 7.00, 2.43, and 1.25 per 100,000 person-years in Clusters I–III, respectively; corresponding Segi-standardised rates were 6.29, 2.03, and 1.09. All three clusters had winter peaks, with additional May–June elevations in Clusters I and II. Only Cluster I showed a statistically significant decline in age-standardised incidence over 2005–2024 (average annual percentage change − 4.28%; 95% confidence interval [CI] − 7.27 to − 2.18). Adults aged ≥ 60 years had the highest incidence among the three broad age groups in each cluster, and incidence in this group increased on average in Cluster III. APC period rate ratios were lower in 2020–2024 than in 2010–2014 across all three clusters, with non-linear cohort variation identified in Cluster I. The vaccination-programme initiation ATT among adults aged 15–59 years was − 1.208 cases per 100,000 (95% CI − 1.994 to − 0.421). Conclusions HFRS burden, seasonality, and age-specific incidence differed across the three clusters. Vaccination-programme initiation was associated with lower county-level incidence in the exploratory analysis. These findings support surveillance and prevention tailored to local burden and seasonal patterns, with continued attention to adults aged ≥ 60 years.
